questions.question: Distinguish population distribution from density, demonstrate the density calculation and its average trap, and explain South Africa's population map through physical and human factors.
questions.expected_answer: Distribution is the pattern of where people are — clustered, dispersed, coastal, empty — while density measures how many per unit of area: total population divided by total area, in people per square kilometre. A region of 3 million people on 25 000 square kilometres has a density of 120 per square kilometre. The trap is that density is an average: Australia's tiny national figure conceals a population crowded onto two coastal fringes, so any density figure should prompt the question of how people are actually arranged within it. Globally, most people live north of the equator in a few dense zones — East Asia, South Asia, Europe, north-eastern North America — on river plains and coasts, while areas too dry (Sahara, Kalahari), too cold (Siberia), too high (Himalayan and Andean plateaus) or too forested and disease-prone (parts of the Amazon and Congo basins) stay near-empty. Physical factors are water above all, then climate, soil, relief and resources; human factors are work, transport, trade, history and politics. South Africa shows both: rainfall thins east to west so people thicken eastward; Gauteng, the smallest province, holds roughly a quarter of the nation on a dry plateau because the 1886 gold discoveries pulled labour, railways and industry there — a human factor overruling the physical; the arid Northern Cape carries about 2 people per square kilometre; harbour cities grew on trade; and apartheid packed millions into former homeland districts on marginal land.

questions.question: Work through the vital rates and the demographic transition, and read a population pyramid in three moves, applying the method to South Africa's pyramid.
questions.expected_answer: The birth rate counts live births per thousand per year and the death rate deaths per thousand; their difference is natural increase, excluding migration — a birth rate of 24 against a death rate of 9 leaves 15 per thousand, or 1.5 per cent per year. The fertility rate is children per woman, with about 2.1 as replacement; the infant mortality rate — deaths under one year per thousand live births — is the most sensitive indicator of living conditions; life expectancy completes the kit. The demographic transition runs: stage one, both rates high, little growth; stage two, death rates fall with clean water, vaccines and food while births stay high — explosion; stage three, birth rates follow down as children survive and women gain education and contraception; stage four, both low, stable; stage five, deaths exceed births and populations shrink and age, as in Japan. Overpopulation is a relationship — more people than local resources support at an acceptable standard — never a raw count. A pyramid stacks age bars, males one side, females the other; read the base for births, the steepness of the sides for survival, and the top for longevity. The wedge shape marks a young, fast-growing, poor population with heavy youth dependency; the block marks a wealthy, ageing one with rising aged dependency. South Africa's pyramid sits between: fertility down to about 2.3 narrowing the base, still youthful, and scarred where the HIV pandemic cut the young-adult bars and lowered life expectancy through the 2000s before the world's largest treatment programme reversed the trend.

questions.question: Explain migration's vocabulary and South Africa's two main flows, then connect urbanisation and informal settlement to the flood risk and water management themes of the year.
questions.expected_answer: Migration is a lasting change of home. One border-crosser is an emigrant leaving and an immigrant arriving; international migration crosses borders while internal migration — dominated by rural-urban movement — stays within them; permanent contrasts with temporary (seasonal workers, commuters) and voluntary with forced (refugees and the internally displaced). Push factors — joblessness, drought, failing services, violence — expel from origins; pull factors — wages, schools, clinics, the reports of earlier migrants — attract to destinations. Internally, young adults leave the former homelands of the Eastern Cape and Limpopo for Gauteng and the coastal metros, ageing the sending regions while remittances flow back and receiving cities strain under housing shortfalls; internationally South Africa draws migrants from Zimbabwe, Mozambique and Lesotho along old mine-labour paths, with tensions that flare as xenophobia. Urbanisation — the rising percentage urban, beyond two thirds in South Africa — outpaces delivery, so informal settlements rise on unclaimed land: steep slopes, industrial margins and floodplains, the land left over because the river built it. Sealed city surfaces and piped stormwater shorten the lag and raise the peak on the hydrograph, wetland loss removes the shock absorbers, and so floods strike hardest where the poorest settled — in minutes on the Jukskei in December 2022, over days across Natal in September 1987. Management answers with dams, the Lesotho Highlands transfer, boreholes, the 6 000-litre free basic allowance, irrigation efficiency ahead of household savings, and the sustainability rule of drawing no faster than renewal — Cape Town's halving of use against Day Zero proving behaviour's power. The year folds into one sentence: people moved for work, settled on the land that was left, and the land that was left belonged to the water.
